evals.prompt: We're Ledgerline, a 60-person B2B SaaS for revenue reconciliation. Our app runs on GCP (we moved off AWS two years ago) but our API edge and backups are on AWS. Most of our deals are 2-3 year enterprise contracts at $150k-400k ACV with banks that have big AWS commitments. Our CRO wants us on AWS Marketplace this quarter because 'customers can burn 100% of their EDP with us'. Engineering wants to register with our existing prod AWS account (it's inside our AWS Organization) and start with pay-as-you-go pricing since it's simplest, then switch to contracts later. Can you sanity check the plan and tell me what to do?
evals.expected_output: A plan that rejects the 100% drawdown promise because the product is not fully on AWS, recommends a fresh standalone seller account, recommends SaaS contract pricing because the pricing model cannot be switched later, and gives a fit verdict.
expectations: States that SaaS not running fully on AWS (application and control plane) does not carry the Deployed on AWS badge and should not be sold as retiring the buyer's EDP/PPA commitment
Refuses to promise a drawdown percentage and says the share is set in each buyer's private AWS contract (or that AWS publishes no cap figure)
Mentions that a fully-on-AWS edition or architecture change is the route to the badge
Recommends a new standalone AWS account for seller registration rather than the production account
States that the seller account becomes seller of record and cannot be changed once a product is listed
Flags the AWS Organizations tax inheritance or legal-entity risk of using an account inside the organization
States that the SaaS pricing model cannot be changed after publishing (to Limited), so starting with pay-as-you-go and switching later would need a new product
Recommends SaaS contract (or contract with consumption) pricing to match multi-year enterprise contracts
Gives an explicit fit verdict (for example list and sell privately without a drawdown promise)
Marks AWS figures with a verify-before-quoting footnote or dagger
Includes an irreversible-choice register or equivalent list naming seller account and pricing model with an owner or decision date

evals.prompt: Quick one. Our biggest customer, Harrow Insurance ($380k/yr, contract renews 1 Feb on our normal paper), asked to renew through AWS Marketplace instead so it counts against their AWS spend. We're fully hosted on AWS. We created our SaaS listing last week (our first and only product) and it's sitting in Limited. My AE wants to send them a private offer from the Limited listing on Monday so it's signed before Christmas, with the new term starting 1 Feb and paid quarterly. What fee do we pay and what do I need to set up?
evals.expected_output: Explains private offers need a public listing (so request Public first, 7-10 business days), flags the renewal so the 1.5% renewal fee applies, uses a future-dated agreement starting 1 Feb with quarterly installments, and runs the buyer pre-check.
expectations: States that private offers require at least one active public listing, so the Limited listing cannot carry the offer
Tells the user to request Public visibility and cites a Seller Operations review of about 7-10 business days
Gives a realistic send date counted forward from the public approval rather than accepting Monday
States the renewal fee is 1.5% rather than the 3% new-deal tier
Tells the user to mark the offer as a renewal of an existing customer moving to AWS Marketplace (offer purpose)
Recommends a future-dated agreement with a service start date of 1 February
Notes that auto-renewal must be off before the future-dated agreement is accepted
Notes the quarterly installment plan needs the buyer to pay by invoice, not card
Tells the user to check whether the buyer runs a Private Marketplace and, if so, to extend the offer to the administrator account as well
Asks for or confirms the buyer's exact 12-digit AWS account ID before sending
Recommends cancelling any test subscriptions before requesting Public

evals.prompt: Enterprise prospect (Northvale Health) wants to buy our platform through AWS Marketplace but only via their reseller, Corbel Systems, who handles all their software. Deal is $500k list for 3 years. We want to give Corbel a 15% margin. Who pays the AWS fees in this setup? Also our ops lead wants to set up the reseller authorization now with loose terms and tighten them later once we know the deal shape.
evals.expected_output: Explains CPPO: ISV issues a selling authorization at a wholesale price, reseller marks up, the tier fee plus 0.5% is computed on the wholesale price and taken from the ISV payout; authorizations cannot be edited later; reseller must be a registered seller.
expectations: Names the mechanism as a Channel Partner Private Offer (CPPO) with a selling or resale authorization from the ISV
States that the ISV sets a wholesale price or discount and the reseller marks it up to the buyer price
States the CPPO fee is the normal tier plus 0.5%
States the fee is computed on the wholesale price to the reseller, not the buyer price
States the fee is deducted from the ISV's payout, not the reseller's
Computes the fee on a $425k wholesale price at 3.5% (about $14,875) or shows equivalent arithmetic
Advises pricing the fee into the partner discount rather than absorbing it
States that a published selling authorization cannot be edited or extended, only deactivated
Recommends a single-buyer authorization tied to Northvale's account for this negotiated deal
States the reseller must itself be a registered paid AWS Marketplace seller

evals.prompt: We listed on AWS Marketplace two months ago and nothing's happened, zero inbound. My VP Sales says AWS reps should be bringing us deals by now. His plan: dump all 120 open opportunities from Salesforce into ACE marked for visibility so AWS sees our pipeline, and apply to ISV Accelerate next week to get their sellers working for us. We've done 1 private offer so far. Does this work?
evals.expected_output: Explains that public listings draw little inbound and AWS sellers do not prospect for unknown ISVs; for-visibility-only opportunities do not count; ISV Accelerate thresholds are not met; gives a ranked co-sell ladder with ACE quality submissions as the default rung.
expectations: States that a public listing alone generates little inbound and revenue comes from private offers on deals the vendor sources
States that AWS sellers do not prospect for an unknown ISV
States that opportunities submitted for visibility only do not count toward ISV Accelerate thresholds or co-sell
Recommends submitting only opportunities with real net-new AWS consumption instead of the whole CRM
Lists ISV Accelerate entry thresholds including 5 launched and 15 qualified opportunities in 12 months
Mentions the Foundational Technical Review (FTR) or Validated status as a prerequisite
Concludes the company does not yet qualify for ISV Accelerate with one private offer
Presents co-sell options as an ordered ranking by effort versus deals unblocked
Names ACE opportunity work as the default rung for now
Mentions responding to AWS-referred opportunities within 5 business days
Sets an expectation of roughly 6-12 months before meaningful AWS field engagement
Recommends linking AWS Partner Central to the Marketplace seller account

evals.prompt: Help. Two AWS Marketplace problems this week. (1) Kestrel Bank says our private offer link shows 'product not available in your private catalog'. We sent it to their account 4411-2290-7718. (2) Our existing customer Pinemoor is mid-way through a 3-year SaaS contract we sold them on Marketplace (paid annually, 2 payments left) and wants 50 more seats now; when we tried a new private offer they got 'You already have an active contract'. Our AE also wants to drop them from 200 to 150 seats on another module at the same time. What do we do?
evals.expected_output: For Kestrel, extend the offer to the Private Marketplace administrator account and get the product approved. For Pinemoor, use an agreement-based replacement offer, carry over the two unbilled annual payments, and explain no mid-term downsizing.
expectations: Diagnoses the Kestrel error as a Private Marketplace restriction
Tells the user to extend the offer to the buyer's Private Marketplace administrator (or management) account as well
Says the buyer's administrator must approve the product in their Private Marketplace
Recommends an agreement-based (replacement or amendment) offer from the Agreements page for Pinemoor
States that the replacement cancels the old agreement's unbilled payments
Tells the user to re-include the two remaining annual payments in the new schedule
States the replacement takes effect on acceptance and cannot be future-dated
States contract buyers cannot reduce quantities mid-term; downsizing happens at renewal
Does not recommend cancelling the contract and reissuing as the first option

evals.prompt: Our CFO has two ideas for AWS Marketplace. First, bump our public listing price by 3% so the Marketplace fee is covered, and take the fee out of the rep's commission on Marketplace deals so it doesn't hit margin. Second, we're raising prices across the board on 1 March and she wants the AWS public price updated the same day for existing public subscribers. Anything wrong with this?
evals.expected_output: Rejects grossing up the public price and deducting the fee from commission; explains the 90-day notice before a public price increase takes effect and the 120-day lock; payout timing after collection.
expectations: Advises against inflating the public price to recover the fee and keeps the public price at list
Recommends handling discounts and deal-specific pricing in private offers
Recommends paying reps the same commission and quota credit on Marketplace deals as direct deals
Explains that deducting the fee from commission makes reps route deals around Marketplace
Recommends crediting reps on offer acceptance
Does not promise that the new price applies to existing public subscribers on 1 March
States a price increase freezes further pricing updates for at least 90 days
Advises submitting any price decreases before the increase, or planning the change well ahead of 1 March
States AWS pays the seller only after collecting from the buyer

evals.prompt: I run a small devtool, a CLI plus hosted dashboard, $29/month per developer, almost all card signups from individual devs and small teams, no sales team. Someone on Twitter said AWS Marketplace is a growth channel because millions of AWS customers browse it. Should I list? I'm on Vercel and Fly.io today.
evals.expected_output: A skip-for-now verdict: self-serve card buyers, no AWS-committed enterprise buyers, no one to own offers, off-AWS hosting; explains listings are a procurement rail, not discovery; gives the condition to revisit.
expectations: Gives a skip or not-now verdict
Explains that the listing is a procurement rail rather than a demand or discovery channel
Cites the absence of enterprise buyers with AWS commitments as a reason
Notes the product is not hosted on AWS so it would not retire buyer commitments
Names a concrete condition for revisiting, such as a named enterprise deal asking to buy through AWS
Does not walk the user through seller registration steps as if listing were recommended
Mentions the ongoing operational cost (integration, offers, owner) rather than the listing fee alone
